AI.motivation: While large language models are increasingly being explored as interfaces between humans and robotic systems, there remains limited evidence on how such technologies can be used not only for interaction, but also as a structured means of introducing robotics to non-specialist users in real organizational settings.
AI.method: A challenge-based method for robotics awareness was implemented through an LLM-enabled humanoid robot activity conducted with employees of AD Ports Group in the UAE. Participants engaged in a team-based, role-driven experience in a logistics-inspired task environment using voice commands interpreted through an LLM-based control framework. The activity was designed to expose participants to embodied AI and human-robot collaboration without requiring prior robotics expertise. A post-event survey was open for 16 days and collected 102 responses to evaluate the approach.
AI.result: Results indicate strong overall reception, with high satisfaction (8.46/10), increased interest in robotics and AI (4.47/5), and improved understanding of emerging forms of human-robot collaboration (4.45/5). Participants who interacted directly with the robot reported natural interaction (4.37/5) and a strong sense that interaction became easier as the activity progressed (4.74/5). Lower ratings for reliability and predictability point to important technical and design challenges for future iterations.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that challenge-based, LLM-enabled humanoid interaction can serve as a promising and replicable method for robotics awareness in industrial and operational environments. The study highlights that while the approach shows strong potential for introducing robotics to non-specialist users, future iterations need to address technical challenges related to reliability and predictability to improve user experience and adoption.

title: From Noise to Intent: Anchoring Generative VLA Policies with Residual Bridges
summary: Bridging high-level semantic understanding with low-level physical control remains a persistent challenge in embodied intelligence, stemming from the fundamental spatiotemporal scale mismatch between cognition and action. Existing generative VLA policies typically adopt a "Generation-from-Noise" paradigm, which disregards this disparity, leading to representation inefficiency and weak condition alignment during optimization. In this work, we propose ResVLA, an architecture that shifts the paradigm to "Refinement-from-Intent." Recognizing that robotic motion naturally decomposes into global intent and local dynamics, ResVLA utilizes spectral analysis to decouple control into a deterministic low-frequency anchor and a stochastic high-frequency residual. By anchoring the generative process on the predicted intent, our model focuses strictly on refining local dynamics via a residual diffusion bridge. Extensive simulation experiments show that ResVLA achieves competitive performance, strong robustness to language and robot embodiment perturbations, and faster convergence than standard generative baselines. It also demonstrates strong performance in real-world robot experiments.

AI.tldr: ResVLA is a novel architecture for embodied intelligence that shifts from "Generation-from-Noise" to "Refinement-from-Intent" by using spectral analysis to decompose robotic motion into a deterministic low-frequency anchor (global intent) and a stochastic high-frequency residual (local dynamics), achieving faster convergence, stronger robustness, and superior performance in both simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the persistent challenge of bridging high-level semantic understanding with low-level physical control in embodied intelligence, stemming from the spatiotemporal scale mismatch between cognition and action. Existing generative Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies use a "Generation-from-Noise" paradigm that disregards this disparity, leading to representation inefficiency and weak condition alignment during optimization.
AI.method: ResVLA proposes a paradigm shift to "Refinement-from-Intent" by utilizing spectral analysis to decouple control into a deterministic low-frequency anchor (representing global intent) and a stochastic high-frequency residual (representing local dynamics). The model anchors the generative process on the predicted intent and employs a residual diffusion bridge to focus strictly on refining local dynamics.
AI.result: Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate that ResVLA achieves competitive performance, strong robustness to language and robot embodiment perturbations, and faster convergence compared to standard generative baselines. Real-world robot experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: ResVLA effectively addresses the spatiotemporal scale mismatch between cognition and action in embodied intelligence, offering a more efficient and robust alternative to existing generative VLA policies. The refinement-from-intent paradigm with spectral-based decomposition of control signals proves superior for bridging semantic understanding with physical control.

title: Ufil: A Unified Framework for Infrastructure-based Localization
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, this work was submitted to IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC) 2026
summary: Infrastructure-based localization enhances road safety and traffic management by providing state estimates of road users. Development is hindered by fragmented, application-specific stacks that tightly couple perception, tracking, and middleware. We introduce Ufil, a Unified Framework for Infrastructure-Based Localization with a standardized object model and reusable multi-object tracking components. Ufil offers interfaces and reference implementations for prediction, detection, association, state update, and track management, allowing researchers to improve components without reimplementing the pipeline. Ufil is open-source C++/ROS 2 software with documentation and executable examples. We demonstrate Ufil by integrating three heterogeneous data sources into a single localization pipeline combining (i) vehicle onboard units broadcasting ETSI ITS-G5 Cooperative Awareness Messages, (ii) a lidar-based roadside sensor node, and (iii) an in-road sensitive surface layer. The pipeline runs unchanged in the CARLA simulator and a small-scale CAV testbed, demonstrating Ufil's scale-independent execution model. In a three-lane highway scenario with 423 and 355 vehicles in simulation and testbed, respectively, the fused system achieves lane-level lateral accuracy with mean lateral position RMSEs of 0.31 m in CARLA and 0.29 m in the CPM Lab, and mean absolute orientation errors around 2.2°. Median end-to-end latencies from sensing to fused output remain below 100 ms across all modalities in both environments.

AI.tldr: Ufil is an open-source C++/ROS 2 framework that provides standardized object models and reusable multi-object tracking components for infrastructure-based localization, enabling integration of heterogeneous data sources with lane-level accuracy and low latency.
AI.motivation: Infrastructure-based localization enhances road safety and traffic management by providing state estimates of road users, but development is hindered by fragmented, application-specific stacks that tightly couple perception, tracking, and middleware.
AI.method: Ufil introduces a Unified Framework with a standardized object model and reusable multi-object tracking components, offering interfaces and reference implementations for prediction, detection, association, state update, and track management. The framework demonstrates scale-independent execution by integrating three heterogeneous data sources (vehicle onboard units broadcasting ETSI ITS-G5 CAMs, a lidar-based roadside sensor node, and an in-road sensitive surface layer) in both CARLA simulator and a CAV testbed.
AI.result: The fused system achieves lane-level lateral accuracy with mean lateral position RMSEs of 0.31 m in CARLA and 0.29 m in the CPM Lab, and mean absolute orientation errors around 2.2°. Median end-to-end latencies from sensing to fused output remain below 100 ms across all modalities.
AI.conclusion: Ufil demonstrates a scalable, modular approach to infrastructure-based localization that enables researchers to improve components without reimplementing the entire pipeline, with proven performance in both simulation and real-world testbeds.

title: MISTY: High-Throughput Motion Planning via Mixer-based Single-step Drifting
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Multi-modal trajectory generation is essential for safe autonomous driving, yet existing diffusion-based planners suffer from high inference latency due to iterative neural function evaluations. This paper presents MISTY (Mixer-based Inference for Single-step Trajectory-drifting Yield), a high-throughput generative motion planner that achieves state-of-the-art closed-loop performance with pure single-step inference. MISTY integrates a vectorized Sub-Graph encoder to capture environment context, a Variational Autoencoder to structure expert trajectories into a compact 32-dimensional latent manifold, and an ultra-lightweight MLP-Mixer decoder to eliminate quadratic attention complexity. Importantly, we introduce a latent-space drifting loss that shifts the complex distribution evolution entirely to the training phase. By formulating explicit attractive and repulsive forces, this mechanism empowers the model to synthesize novel, proactive maneuvers, such as active overtaking, that are virtually absent from the raw expert demonstrations. Extensive evaluations on the nuPlan benchmark demonstrate that MISTY achieves state-of-the-art results on the challenging Test14-hard split, with comprehensive scores of 80.32 and 82.21 in non-reactive and reactive settings, respectively. Operating at over 99 FPS with an end-to-end latency of 10.1 ms, MISTY offers an order-of-magnitude speedup over iterative diffusion planners while while achieving significantly robust generation.

AI.tldr: MISTY is a high-throughput single-step generative motion planner for autonomous driving that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the nuPlan benchmark with over 99 FPS and 10.1 ms latency, using a vectorized Sub-Graph encoder, VAE-based latent representation, MLP-Mixer decoder, and latent-space drifting loss for novel maneuver synthesis.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal trajectory generation is essential for safe autonomous driving, but existing diffusion-based planners suffer from high inference latency due to iterative neural function evaluations.
AI.method: MISTY integrates: 1) a vectorized Sub-Graph encoder for environment context, 2) a Variational Autoencoder to structure expert trajectories into a 32-dimensional latent manifold, and 3) an ultra-lightweight MLP-Mixer decoder to eliminate quadratic attention complexity. It introduces a latent-space drifting loss with explicit attractive and repulsive forces to shift complex distribution evolution to the training phase, enabling synthesis of novel proactive maneuvers like active overtaking.
AI.result: On the nuPlan benchmark Test14-hard split, MISTY achieves comprehensive scores of 80.32 (non-reactive) and 82.21 (reactive), operating at over 99 FPS with 10.1 ms end-to-end latency, offering an order-of-magnitude speedup over iterative diffusion planners.
AI.conclusion: MISTY demonstrates that single-step inference with proper latent-space modeling can achieve state-of-the-art closed-loop performance with significantly reduced computational cost, enabling practical deployment in real-time autonomous driving systems.

title: X2-N: A Transformable Wheel-legged Humanoid Robot with Dual-mode Locomotion and Manipulation
summary:
Wheel-legged robots combine the efficiency of wheeled locomotion with the versatility of legged systems, enabling rapid traversal over both continuous and discrete terrains. However, conventional designs typically employ fixed wheels as feet and limited degrees of freedom (DoFs) at the hips, resulting in reduced stability and mobility during legged locomotion compared to humanoids with flat feet. In addition, most existing platforms lack a full upper body with arms, which limits their ability to perform dexterous manipulation tasks.
  In this letter, we present X2-N, a high-DoF transformable robot with dual-mode locomotion and manipulation. X2-N can operate in both humanoid and wheel-legged forms and transform seamlessly between them through joint reconfiguration. We further propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based whole-body control framework tailored to this morphology, enabling unified control across hybrid locomotion, transformation, and manipulation. We validate X2-N in a range of challenging locomotion and manipulation tasks, including dynamic skating-like motion, stair climbing and package delivery. Results demonstrate high locomotion efficiency, strong terrain adaptability, and stable loco-manipulation performance of X2-N, highlighting its potential for real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: X2-N is a high-DoF transformable robot that seamlessly transitions between humanoid and wheel-legged forms, using RL-based whole-body control for unified locomotion and manipulation tasks including dynamic skating, stair climbing, and package delivery.
AI.motivation: Conventional wheel-legged robots have fixed wheels as feet, limited hip DOFs, reduced stability compared to humanoids, and lack upper bodies for manipulation. This limits their effectiveness in both locomotion and dexterous tasks.
AI.method: X2-N is a high-DoF transformable robot with dual-mode locomotion and manipulation capabilities. It operates in both humanoid and wheel-legged forms, transforming seamlessly via joint reconfiguration. A reinforcement learning-based whole-body control framework enables unified control across hybrid locomotion, transformation, and manipulation.
AI.result: Validated in dynamic skating-like motion, stair climbing, and package delivery tasks. Demonstrates high locomotion efficiency, strong terrain adaptability, and stable loco-manipulation performance.
AI.conclusion: X2-N shows strong potential for real-world deployment due to its efficient traversal of both continuous and discrete terrains, effective loco-manipulation capabilities, and seamless transformation between locomotion modes.

title: A Bayesian Reasoning Framework for Robotic Systems in Autonomous Casualty Triage
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: Autonomous robots deployed in mass casualty incidents (MCI) face the challenge of making critical decisions based on incomplete and noisy perceptual data. We present an autonomous robotic system for casualty assessment that fuses outputs from multiple vision-based algorithms, estimating signs of severe hemorrhage, visible trauma, or physical alertness, into a coherent triage assessment. At the core of our system is a Bayesian network, constructed from expert-defined rules, which enables probabilistic reasoning about a casualty's condition even with missing or conflicting sensory inputs. The system, evaluated during the DARPA Triage Challenge (DTC) in realistic MCI scenarios involving 11 and 9 casualties, demonstrated a nearly three-fold improvement in physiological assessment accuracy (from 15\% to 42\% and 19\% to 46\%) compared to a vision-only baseline. More importantly, overall triage accuracy increased from 14\% to 53\%, while the diagnostic coverage of the system expanded from 31\% to 95\% of cases. These results demonstrate that integrating expert-guided probabilistic reasoning with advanced vision-based sensing can significantly enhance the reliability and decision-making capabilities of autonomous systems in critical real-world applications.

AI.tldr: An autonomous robotic system for casualty assessment in mass casualty incidents (MCI) fuses multiple vision-based algorithms via a Bayesian network to improve physiological assessment accuracy from 15-19% to 42-46% and overall triage accuracy from 14% to 53%, while expanding diagnostic coverage from 31% to 95%.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots deployed in mass casualty incidents face challenges making critical decisions based on incomplete and noisy perceptual data, necessitating more robust assessment capabilities.
AI.method: The system fuses outputs from multiple vision-based algorithms (detecting severe hemorrhage, visible trauma, and physical alertness) using a Bayesian network constructed from expert-defined rules, enabling probabilistic reasoning about casualty conditions despite missing or conflicting sensory inputs.
AI.result: Evaluated during the DARPA Triage Challenge in realistic MCI scenarios with 11 and 9 casualties, demonstrating nearly three-fold improvement in physiological assessment accuracy (15%→42% and 19%→46%) compared to vision-only baseline, with overall triage accuracy increasing from 14% to 53% and diagnostic coverage expanding from 31% to 95%.
AI.conclusion: Integrating expert-guided probabilistic reasoning with advanced vision-based sensing significantly enhances the reliability and decision-making capabilities of autonomous systems in critical real-world applications.

title: SLAM as a Stochastic Control Problem with Partial Information: Optimal Solutions and Rigorous Approximations
summary: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a foundational state estimation problem in robotics in which a robot accurately constructs a map of its environment while also localizing itself within this construction. We study the active SLAM problem through the lens of optimal stochastic control, thereby recasting it as a decision-making problem under partial information. After reviewing several commonly studied models, we present a general stochastic control formulation of active SLAM together with a rigorous treatment of motion, sensing, and map representation. We introduce a new exploration stage cost that encodes the geometry of the state when evaluating information-gathering actions. This formulation, constructed as a nonstandard partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), is then analyzed to derive rigorously justified approximate solutions that are near-optimal. To enable this analysis, the associated regularity conditions are studied under general assumptions that apply to a wide range of robotics applications. For a particular case, we conduct an extensive numerical study in which standard learning algorithms are used to learn near-optimal policies.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates active SLAM as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) using optimal stochastic control theory, introduces a geometry-aware exploration cost, derives near-optimal approximate solutions under general regularity conditions, and validates the approach through numerical experiments demonstrating that standard learning algorithms can discover near-optimal exploration policies.
AI.motivation: Active SLAM—where a robot decides where to explore to improve its map and self-localization—is a decision-making problem under partial information that lacks a rigorous mathematical foundation. The authors aim to bridge this gap by recasting active SLAM as an optimal stochastic control problem, enabling principled analysis and computation of exploration strategies.
AI.method: The authors develop a general stochastic control formulation of active SLAM as a nonstandard POMDP. Key components include: (1) a review of commonly studied SLAM models, (2) a rigorous treatment of motion dynamics, sensing models, and map representations, (3) introduction of a new exploration stage cost that encodes the geometry of the state space, and (4) analysis of regularity conditions under general assumptions applicable to diverse robotics applications. The framework then yields provably near-optimal approximate solutions.
AI.result: The proposed POMDP formulation with geometry-aware exploration cost satisfies general regularity conditions enabling rigorous analysis. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that standard learning algorithms can learn near-optimal policies for this active SLAM problem, validating the theoretical framework.
AI.conclusion: The stochastic control formulation with geometry-aware exploration cost provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for active SLAM, enabling the derivation of provably near-optimal exploration policies. This approach bridges the gap between theoretical control theory and practical robotic exploration, offering a principled framework that can be applied across a wide range of SLAM scenarios.

title: Effects of Swarm Size Variability on Operator Workload
summary: Real-world deployments of human--swarm teams depend on balancing operator workload to leverage human strengths without inducing overload. A key challenge is that swarm size is often dynamic: robots may join or leave the mission due to failures or redeployment, causing abrupt workload fluctuations. Understanding how such changes affect human workload and performance is critical for robust human--swarm interaction design. This paper investigates how the magnitude and direction of changes in swarm size influence operator workload. Drawing on the concept of workload history, we test three hypotheses: (1) workload remains elevated following decreases in swarm size, (2) small increases are more manageable than large jumps, and (3) sufficiently large changes override these effects by inducing a cognitive reset. We conducted two studies (N = 34) using a monitoring task with simulated drone swarms of varying sizes. By varying the swarm size between episodes, we measured perceived workload relative to swarm size changes. Results show that objective performance is largely unaffected by small changes in swarm size, while subjective workload is sensitive to both change direction and magnitude. Small increases preserve lower workload, whereas small decreases leave workload elevated, indicating workload residue; large changes in either direction attenuate these effects, suggesting a reset response. These findings offer actionable guidance for managing swarm-size transitions to support operator workload in dynamic human--swarm systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how changes in swarm size (magnitude and direction) affect operator workload in human-swarm teams, finding that workload is sensitive to these changes and that large changes can cause cognitive resets.
AI.motivation: Real-world deployments of human-swarm teams face workload balancing challenges, particularly when swarm size changes dynamically due to failures or redeployment. Understanding how these changes affect human workload and performance is critical for interaction design.
AI.method: Two studies (N = 34) using a monitoring task with simulated drone swarms of varying sizes. Swarm size was varied between episodes to measure perceived workload relative to size changes. Three hypotheses were tested: (1) workload remains elevated following decreases in swarm size, (2) small increases are more manageable than large jumps, and (3) sufficiently large changes override these effects by inducing a cognitive reset.
AI.result: Objective performance was largely unaffected by small changes in swarm size, while subjective workload was sensitive to both change direction and magnitude. Small increases preserve lower workload, whereas small decreases leave workload elevated (workload residue), and large changes in either direction attenuate these effects (suggesting a reset response).
AI.conclusion: The findings offer actionable guidance for managing swarm-size transitions to support operator workload in dynamic human-swarm systems.

title: A Compact Peristaltic Pump Based on Magneto-Elastic Hysteresis with Single Pneumatic Control
comment: 5 pages
summary: Pumping fluids is fundamental to a wide range of industrial, environmental, and biomedical applications. Among various pumping mechanisms, peristaltic pumps enable efficient and safe fluid transport by deforming an elastic tube without direct contact with the working fluid. Although previous studies have introduced mechanical, pneumatic, or magnetic actuations to drive membrane deformation, these approaches often lead to complex pump architectures and control schemes. In this study, we present a soft membrane pump that achieves peristaltic motion through a single pneumatic input combined with an embedded passive magnet. The actuation mechanism and system dynamics were analyzed and simplified through modeling. Numerical simulations were conducted to predict the internal fluid flow, and the magneto-elastic hysteresis behavior observed in the simulations was successfully validated by experiments with a proof-of-concept prototype.

AI.tldr: A soft membrane pump uses a single pneumatic input combined with an embedded passive magnet to achieve peristaltic motion for fluid transport. The actuation mechanism and system dynamics were modeled, and numerical simulations predicting internal fluid flow and magneto-elastic hysteresis behavior were experimentally validated.
AI.motivation: Peristaltic pumps are essential for industrial, environmental, and biomedical fluid transport. Previous actuation methods (mechanical, pneumatic, magnetic) often lead to complex pump architectures and control schemes. A simpler actuation mechanism is needed.
AI.method: A soft membrane pump designed with single pneumatic input and embedded passive magnet to achieve peristaltic motion. Actuation mechanism and system dynamics were analyzed through modeling. Numerical simulations predicted internal fluid flow. A proof-of-concept prototype was fabricated for experimental validation.
AI.result: Numerical simulations successfully predicted internal fluid flow and magneto-elastic hysteresis behavior, which was experimentally validated using the proof-of-concept prototype.
AI.conclusion: The proposed soft membrane pump achieves efficient peristaltic motion through a simple combination of pneumatic actuation and embedded passive magnet, with modeling and experimental validation confirming the design's effectiveness.

title: Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training
comment: Project Page: https://hi-wm.github.io/
summary: Post-training is essential for turning pretrained generalist robot policies into reliable task-specific controllers, but existing human-in-the-loop pipelines remain tied to physical execution: each correction requires robot time, scene setup, resets, and operator supervision in the real world. Meanwhile, action-conditioned world models have been studied mainly for imagination, synthetic data generation, and policy evaluation. We propose \textbf{Human-in-the-World-Model (Hi-WM)}, a post-training framework that uses a learned world model as a reusable corrective substrate for failure-targeted policy improvement. A policy is first rolled out in closed loop inside the world model; when the rollout becomes incorrect or failure-prone, a human intervenes directly in the model to provide short corrective actions. Hi-WM caches intermediate states and supports rollback and branching, allowing a single failure state to be reused for multiple corrective continuations and yielding dense supervision around behaviors that the base policy handles poorly. The resulting corrective trajectories are then added back to the training set for post-training. We evaluate Hi-WM on three real-world manipulation tasks spanning both rigid and deformable object interaction, and on two policy backbones. Hi-WM improves real-world success by 37.9 points on average over the base policy and by 19.0 points over a world-model closed-loop baseline, while world-model evaluation correlates strongly with real-world performance (r = 0.953). These results suggest that world models can serve not only as generators or evaluators, but also as effective corrective substrates for scalable robot post-training.

AI.tldr: Hi-WM is a post-training framework that uses a learned world model as a corrective substrate, allowing humans to intervene directly in the model to improve robot policies, with significant gains in real-world success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing human-in-the-loop pipelines require physical execution, which is time-consuming and requires robot time, scene setup, resets, and operator supervision. Action-conditioned world models have been studied mainly for imagination, synthetic data generation, and policy evaluation, not as corrective substrates for post-training.
AI.method: Hi-WM rolls out a policy in closed loop inside a learned world model; when the rollout becomes incorrect or failure-prone, a human intervenes directly in the model to provide short corrective actions. The model caches intermediate states and supports rollback and branching, allowing a single failure state to be reused for multiple corrective continuations. The resulting corrective trajectories are added back to the training set for post-training.
AI.result: Hi-WM improved real-world success by 37.9 points on average over the base policy and by 19.0 points over a world-model closed-loop baseline. World-model evaluation correlated strongly with real-world performance (r = 0.953).
AI.conclusion: World models can serve not only as generators or evaluators, but also as effective corrective substrates for scalable robot post-training, enabling dense supervision around behaviors that base policies handle poorly without requiring physical execution.

title: VistaBot: View-Robust Robot Manipulation via Spatiotemporal-Aware View Synthesis
comment: This paper has been accepted to ICRA 2026
summary: Recently, end-to-end robotic manipulation models have gained significant attention for their generalizability and scalability. However, they often suffer from limited robustness to camera viewpoint changes when training with a fixed camera. In this paper, we propose VistaBot, a novel framework that integrates feed-forward geometric models with video diffusion models to achieve view-robust closed-loop manipulation without requiring camera calibration at test time. Our approach consists of three key components: 4D geometry estimation, view synthesis latent extraction, and latent action learning. VistaBot is integrated into both action-chunking (ACT) and diffusion-based ($π_0$) policies and evaluated across simulation and real-world tasks. We further introduce the View Generalization Score (VGS) as a new metric for comprehensive evaluation of cross-view generalization. Results show that VistaBot improves VGS by 2.79$\times$ and 2.63$\times$ over ACT and $π_0$, respectively, while also achieving high-quality novel view synthesis. Our contributions include a geometry-aware synthesis model, a latent action planner, a new benchmark metric, and extensive validation across diverse environments. The code and models will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: VistaBot integrates feed-forward geometric models with video diffusion models to achieve view-robust closed-loop manipulation without camera calibration at test time, improving cross-view generalization by 2.79× (ACT) and 2.63× (π0).
AI.motivation: End-to-end robotic manipulation models suffer from limited robustness to camera viewpoint changes when trained with fixed cameras.
AI.method: VistaBot consists of three key components: 4D geometry estimation, view synthesis latent extraction, and latent action learning, integrated into both ACT and diffusion-based (π0) policies.
AI.result: VistaBot improves the View Generalization Score (VGS) by 2.79× over ACT and 2.63× over π0, while achieving high-quality novel view synthesis.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a geometry-aware synthesis model, a latent action planner, a new benchmark metric (VGS), and extensive validation across diverse simulation and real-world environments.
